name: ESP32-S3-MINI-1-N8
title: ESP32-S3-MINI-1 / MINI-1U: 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE 5 module, dual-core LX7, up to 8 MB flash
summary: A small surface-mount radio module built on the ESP32-S3 system-on-chip: two Xtensa LX7 cores at up to 240 MHz, 802.11b/g/n Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz and Bluetooth 5 LE, with a 40 MHz crystal, quad-SPI flash and the RF matching inside a shielded can. The MINI-1 has an antenna etched on its own board (15.4 × 20.5 × 2.4 mm); the MINI-1U has a miniature coaxial socket for an external antenna instead (15.4 × 15.4 × 2.4 mm). The -N8 versions carry 8 MB of flash and no PSRAM; the -N4R2 versions carry 4 MB of flash and 2 MB of PSRAM. It runs from one 3.0 to 3.6 V supply, brings out 39 GPIOs on 65 land pads, and is rated for -40 to 85 °C ambient.
key_figures: ESP32-S3 (ESP32-S3FN8 in -N8, ESP32-S3FH4R2 in -N4R2), dual-core Xtensa LX7, up to 240 MHz
384 KB ROM, 512 KB SRAM, 16 KB RTC SRAM
8 MB quad SPI, no PSRAM (-N8); 4 MB flash + 2 MB PSRAM (-N4R2)
3.0 ~ 3.6 V, supply able to deliver 0.5 A
7 µA typ (RTC memory on, RTC peripherals off)

notes: MINI-1 carries a PCB antenna and MINI-1U a connector for an external antenna. In each type the -N8 and -N4R2 versions differ in flash and PSRAM size.
The flash runs at no more than 80 MHz clock by default and has no auto-suspend; a 120 MHz clock or auto-suspend is available from Espressif on request.
Ambient temperature is that of the air right around the module.
ESP32-S3FN8 holds 8 MB flash in its package; ESP32-S3FH4R2 holds 4 MB flash and 2 MB PSRAM.

circuits.title: Typical application: supply, reset, boot, UART, JTAG, USB and 32 kHz crystal
circuits.description: The module on its base board with the parts round it. The 3.3 V rail feeds 3V3 with 22 µF and 0.1 µF to ground. EN gets an RC start-up delay (R1 to the rail, C2 to ground, values left to the designer; 10 kΩ and 1 µF is the usual start) and a reset push button, SW1 with 0.1 µF across it, reaching EN through a 0 Ω link. A two-pin jumper pulls IO0 to ground to enter download mode. A four-pin UART header carries VDD33, RXD0, TXD0 and ground, and a second four-pin header brings out TMS, TDI, TDO and TCK on IO42, IO41, IO40 and IO39. A two-pin USB OTG header meets IO20 (D+) and IO19 (D-) through 0 Ω links, with an optional capacitor to ground on each line. An optional 32.768 kHz crystal with 12 pF loads can sit on IO15/IO16 through 0 Ω links; it and its parts are not fitted by default. The other GPIOs are free.

parts.note: EN pull-up of the RC delay; 10 kΩ is the usual value
EN capacitor of the RC delay; 1 µF is the usual value

notes: NC marks a position left empty by default.
Soldering the centre ground pad to the base board ground is optional and improves heat flow; too much paste there lifts the module and can spoil the joints on the edge pads.
The EN RC values are tuned to the supply's power-up behaviour and the chip's power-up and reset timing.

operation.text: The module holds the ESP32-S3 SoC with its flash (and, in -N4R2, PSRAM) in the same package, a 40 MHz crystal, the RF matching network and either the PCB antenna (MINI-1) or the antenna socket (MINI-1U). Apart from the GPIOs, the module's connections are the 3V3 supply input and EN.

Inside, the 3.3 V rail is decoupled by 10 µF, 1 µF and two 0.1 µF capacitors, with a 2.0 nH (±0.1 nH) series inductor feeding the VDD3P3 pins (2 and 3) and a further 1 µF and 10 nF at the analogue supply; an ESD diode sits on the rail. The 40 MHz crystal is ±10 ppm with load capacitors chosen for the crystal, and its feed has a series element (resistor or inductor, 24 nH to begin with) tuned to the board. The antenna feed is a 50 Ω controlled-impedance line through a matching network whose values depend on the board (L3, C5, C11, L2 and C12 on the MINI-1; C11, L2 and C12 on the MINI-1U). VDD_SPI is decoupled by 0.1 µF and 1 µF. U0TXD has a 499 Ω series resistor, and GPIO45 has a 10 kΩ pull-up position that is not fitted.

Two 32-bit Xtensa LX7 cores with single-precision FPU run at up to 240 MHz, with 384 KB ROM, 512 KB SRAM and 16 KB SRAM in the RTC domain. The CPU can be shut down while the low-power co-processor watches peripherals for changes or thresholds.

Wi-Fi is 802.11b/g/n on channels 2412 to 2484 MHz, up to 150 Mbps on 802.11n, with A-MPDU and A-MSDU aggregation and 0.4 µs guard interval. Bluetooth is LE 5 with mesh, at 125 Kbps, 500 Kbps, 1 Mbps and 2 Mbps, with advertising extensions, multiple advertisement sets and channel selection algorithm #2. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth share the antenna through an internal coexistence scheme. RF figures are taken at the antenna port (a cable on the MINI-1U, 50 Ω external antenna), including front-end loss; channel range and transmit power are set in software.

Four pins are sampled into latches at power-up or hardware reset and hold their values until the chip powers down: GPIO0 and GPIO46 choose the boot mode, GPIO45 the VDD_SPI voltage, GPIO46 ROM message printing, and GPIO3 the JTAG source. After reset they are ordinary I/O. External pull resistors, or a host MCU, set a level other than the default. Each setting also depends on eFuse bits, all 0 when shipped; an eFuse burnt to 1 stays 1.

In SPI Boot the ROM loader runs the program from SPI flash. In Joint Download Boot a binary can be written to flash, or loaded into SRAM and run there, over UART0 or USB. The chip also has an SPI Download Boot mode.
During boot the ROM prints to UART0 and the USB Serial/JTAG controller by default; either output can be switched off by register and eFuse settings, leaving USB Serial/JTAG only or UART0 only.
GPIO3 picks the JTAG source early in boot together with three eFuses. It has no pull resistor of its own, so whatever drives it must hold a firm level.

EN is raised only once the supply rails have settled (tSTBL, 50 µs min after the supply reaches 2.8 V). Holding EN below VIL_nRST for at least 50 µs (tRST) resets the chip. An RC delay on EN, usually 10 kΩ and 1 µF, keeps the chip in reset until its supply is steady.

Three UARTs up to 5 Mbps with RS485 and IrDA, sharing 1024 × 8-bit FIFO RAM; two I2C controllers (100 kbit/s, 400 kbit/s, up to 800 kbit/s depending on pull-up strength, 7- and 10-bit addressing); two I2S interfaces (8 to 32 bit, BCK 10 kHz to 40 MHz, TDM and PDM); an LCD interface (8 to 16 bit RGB, I8080, MOTO6800, 40 MHz or lower) and a DVP camera interface (8 to 16 bit, up to 40 MHz); SPI0/SPI1 for flash and PSRAM (up to 120 MHz in 8-line SDR/DDR) and general SPI2 and SPI3 (master up to 80 MHz, slave up to 60 MHz; SPI2 has six chip selects, SPI3 three); a TWAI controller compatible with ISO 11898-1 (CAN 2.0), 1 Kbit/s to 1 Mbit/s with a 64-byte receive FIFO; full-speed USB 2.0 OTG with integrated transceiver; a USB Serial/JTAG controller (CDC-ACM plus JTAG, can reset the chip and enter download mode from the host); an SD/MMC host up to 80 MHz with 1-, 4- and 8-bit buses; LED PWM with up to 14-bit duty resolution; two MCPWM units each with three timers, three operators and a capture module; an RMT with four TX and four RX channels sharing 384 × 32-bit RAM; and four 16-bit pulse counters. Not every chip signal reaches a module pad.

Two 12-bit SAR ADCs measure 20 channels and can be run by the ULP co-processor in sleep to wake the CPU on a threshold. The temperature sensor spans -40 °C to 125 °C and reports the die temperature, which sits above ambient and moves with clock speed and I/O load. Fourteen GPIOs work as capacitive touch inputs; the touch sensor has not yet passed conducted-susceptibility testing.
At 80 MHz the SD/MMC clock phase can only be 0° or 180°, so board layout has to close the timing.

No antenna ships with the module. Certification used a third-generation monopole antenna, material code TFPD08H10060011, of 2.33 dBi gain. A replacement suits the 2.4 GHz band, is 50 Ω, has no more than 2.33 dBi peak gain and mates with the module's socket; another antenna type or gain may need further testing such as EMC.
The MINI-1 has an antenna keepout zone above its top pad row; the base board should disturb the module's antenna as little as possible. The MINI-1U has no keepout zone.
Reflow once only. Keep the module away from ultrasonic welding or cleaning: the vibration can resonate the internal crystal and degrade or stop the module.
